USMLE-style practice · Pharmacology

Fentanyl: 2

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

An opioid-naive patient requests a fentanyl patch for a recent minor injury. Which prescribing principle explains why the patch is unsuitable despite fentanyl being an effective analgesic in appropriately selected clinical circumstances?

  1. QT prolongation and torsades risk
  2. Reserve the patch for appropriately opioid-tolerant patients
  3. Support ventilation and obtain emergency care
  4. Recurrent toxicity after antagonist effect wanes
  5. Precipitated opioid withdrawal
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Reserve the patch for appropriately opioid-tolerant patients

Transdermal fentanyl is not suitable for opioid-naive patients or routine acute pain.

Understanding the options

Reserve the patch for appropriately opioid-tolerant patients
Transdermal fentanyl is not suitable for opioid-naive patients or routine acute pain.
Support ventilation and obtain emergency care
Airway and breathing support accompany overdose reversal; naloxone does not replace resuscitation. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Recurrent toxicity after antagonist effect wanes
Many opioids last longer than naloxone, so repeat dosing and monitoring may be needed. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Precipitated opioid withdrawal
An antagonist or high-affinity partial agonist can abruptly reduce receptor stimulation in a dependent patient. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
QT prolongation and torsades risk
Methadone can prolong repolarization; interacting medicines and electrolyte abnormalities increase concern. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
